newsitem.title: USA: Mob turncoat Gravano takes stand in New York City.
newsitem.headline: Mob turncoat Gravano takes stand in New York City.

text.p: Famed Mafia turncoat Salvatore "Sammy the Bull" Gravano came out of hiding on Thursday to give damning testimony against another accused mobster, Vincent "The Chin" Gigante.
Gravano, whose testimony about life in organised crime helped convict Gambino godfather John Gotti in 1992, identified Gigante as head of the Genovese crime family.
Gravano testified that as a former captain and later underboss of the Gambino family, he often met with Gigante.
"Chin was the boss," he said. Gigante faces a 21-count murder and racketeering indictment in Brooklyn federal court.
Gravano, 52, appeared nervous and looked anxiously around the courtroom at first but relaxed visibly as the day wore on.
His hair slightly grayer and thinner than in his picture on the cover of his recently published memoirs, "Underboss," he wore a stylish, steel-gray suit and small, round glasses.
In soft, matter-of-fact tones, he spoke about life as a mobster.

"At that time my crimes were labour racketeering, I had some clubs, gambling clubs, loan sharking, murders, that type of thing," Gravano said in his Brooklyn, New York, accent under questioning by a prosecutor.
Gravano confessed to 19 murders as part of a 1991 deal with the government to testify against reputed mobsters for at least two years. He spent five years in prison.
He has left the federal witness protection programme but remains in hiding.
Facing him in the front row of the Brooklyn federal courtroom were several relatives of his murder victims, whose grisly demises he recounts in his book.
"He looks uncomfortable," said Laura Garafolo, 24, whose father Eddie was killed by Gravano in 1990. "Then again, his choice in life is his own decision."

"He obviously knows we're here," she added. Prosecutors at one point complained to U.S. District Judge Jack Weinstein that victims' relatives seated themselves around the courtroom in an effort to intimidate the government's star witness.
Gigante sat quietly in a wheelchair, muttering to himself.
His attorneys say he has been incapacitated by mental illness for years, but prosecutors say he has feigned illness to avoid prosecution.
One of New York's last old-time reputed mob dons, Gigante has been known recently for wandering around the Greenwich Village neighbourhood wearing a tattered bathrobe and slippers.
Gravano testified that Gigante once attended a meeting unshaven in pajamas and a bathrobe but was lucid. At other times, Gigante wore street clothes, he said.
Gigante is accused of ordering the killing of seven people and conspiring to kill three others, allegedly to avenge breaches of protocol such as unauthorised slayings.
Gravano reportedly was reluctant to testify because he was concerned about possible questions about payment for his book, which he wrote in collaboration with author Peter Maas.

But the judge blocked a bid by the families of Gravano's victims and the New York State Attorney General to serve legal papers on Gravano when he came to court. The judge said witnesses such as Gravano must be protected from such encounters.
Under New York's so-called "Son of Sam" law, which limits the ability of convicted criminals to profit from accounts of their crimes, Gravano could not keep any money he was paid.
Published reports have said Gravano earned as much as six figures from the book deal, but both Maas and publisher Harper Collins have denied paying him for his story.
The trial is expected to continue for another three weeks. If convicted, Gigante faces the possibility of life in prison.
